title: Mock 1
description: A quarter length SSAT in the real running order: writing sample first, then Quantitative, Reading, Verbal and a second Quantitative section. Five answer choices throughout, and wrong answers cost a quarter point. Take this cold.

writing.name: Writing sample
writing.note: Not scored, but a copy goes to every school that receives your results. Middle Level gives you two creative starters. Pick one, plan for a few minutes, and write a story.
prompts: The door had been locked for as long as anyone could remember.
She knew it was a mistake the moment she said yes.

questions.stem: If 4x - 3 = 17, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Add 3 to both sides to get 4x = 20, then divide by 4 to get x = 5. Checking backwards is faster than solving on a test like this: 4 times 5 is 20, minus 3 is 17.

questions.stem: What is 3/5 of 45?
questions.explanation: One fifth of 45 is 9, so three fifths is 27. The choice 9 is only one fifth, and 75 is what you get by dividing by 3 and multiplying by 5, which reverses the fraction.

questions.stem: A number is increased by 20% and becomes 60. What was the original number?
questions.explanation: After a 20% increase the number is 120% of the original, so the original is 60 divided by 1.2, which is 50. The choice 48 is what you get by taking 20% off 60 instead, and that is the trap the question is built around: a 20% rise and a 20% fall are not opposites.

questions.stem: The perimeter of a square is 28. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Each side is 28 divided by 4, which is 7, so the area is 7 times 7, or 49. The choice 56 is double the perimeter and 64 is the area of a square with side 8.

questions.stem: A rectangle's length is 3 more than its width, and its perimeter is 26. What is the width?
questions.explanation: Let the width be w. Then the length is w + 3, and the perimeter is 2(w + w + 3) = 4w + 6 = 26. So 4w = 20 and w = 5. The choice 8 is the length, and answering with the wrong one of the two is the usual slip.

questions.stem: The average of five numbers is 12. When one number is removed, the average of the remaining four is 13. What was the number removed?
questions.explanation: Five numbers averaging 12 total 60. Four numbers averaging 13 total 52. The removed number is 60 minus 52, which is 8. Notice it is below the original average, which is why the average of the rest went up.

p1: A lichen looks like a single plant, but it is not a plant and it is not single. Each one is a partnership between a fungus and an alga, two organisms from entirely different kingdoms, living so closely intertwined that for centuries nobody suspected there were two of them at all.

The arrangement suits both. The fungus builds the structure and holds water, which is why lichens survive on bare rock, on gravestones, on the frozen ground of the Arctic. The alga, sheltered inside, does the photosynthesis and feeds them both. Neither could live in those places alone.

When the botanist Simon Schwendener proposed this idea in 1869, his colleagues did not merely disagree. They ridiculed him. The notion that a respectable organism might be two creatures in a permanent arrangement struck them as absurd, even faintly improper. It took decades of patient work by others before the partnership was accepted, and more than a century before anyone realised that many lichens contain a third partner, a yeast, that nobody had noticed either.
p2: My grandmother kept the good scissors in a drawer that stuck, and she was the only one allowed to open it. I understood this to be a rule of the universe, like gravity, and I did not question it until I was nine.

That summer she started forgetting things. Small ones at first: where she had left her glasses, whether she had already told me about the neighbour's dog. Then one afternoon she asked me to fetch the good scissors, and I stood in front of the drawer for a long moment before I pulled it open.

Inside were the scissors, a ball of string, three buttons, and a photograph of a young woman standing beside a bicycle, laughing at somebody outside the frame. I brought her the scissors and said nothing about the photograph. She cut the thread, handed them back, and told me to put them away properly.
I did. I have thought about that photograph nearly every week since, and I never asked her about it, and now there is no one left to ask.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about
choices: an organism that turned out to be a partnership, and how slowly that was accepted
the differences between plants and algae
questions.explanation: The passage explains the partnership, then spends its final paragraph on how long it took anyone to believe it. Choice C is a detail used as evidence, and choice D takes one name and inflates it into the subject, which is the most common wrong answer on main idea questions.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the fungus contributes
questions.explanation: The second paragraph splits the labour: the fungus builds the structure and holds water, and the alga does the photosynthesis. Choice B swaps the two partners, which is the trap.

questions.stem: As used in the final paragraph, the word improper most nearly means
questions.explanation: The word sits alongside ridiculed and absurd, and the sentence is describing an emotional reaction to the idea rather than a technical objection. The scientists found it not just wrong but distasteful. Context, not the dictionary entry you know best, decides these.

questions.stem: The final sentence, about a third partner nobody had noticed, mainly serves to
choices: prove that Schwendener was wrong after all
argue that lichens are the most complex organisms
suggest that even settled scientific knowledge can still be incomplete
questions.explanation: The sentence extends the pattern of the whole passage: something was there all along and nobody saw it. It does not undo Schwendener, it repeats his lesson. Ask what a sentence is doing in the passage, not only what it says.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Schwendener's colleagues is best described as
questions.explanation: The phrase did not merely disagree, they ridiculed him carries clear disapproval, but the tone stays measured rather than angry. On tone questions the answer is usually the mild option, because passages chosen for tests rarely shout. Furious is too strong and neutral ignores the wording.

questions.stem: The narrator's statement that the rule about the drawer was like gravity suggests that
choices: as a young child the narrator accepted the rule without question
questions.explanation: Comparing a household rule to a law of physics is a way of saying it seemed permanent and beyond questioning. The next sentence confirms it: the narrator did not question it until nine. Figurative language questions ask what the comparison is doing, never what it literally says.

questions.stem: Why does the narrator stand in front of the drawer for a long moment?
choices: The drawer was stuck and would not open
The narrator had forgotten what was wanted
Opening it meant breaking a rule that had always held
The narrator was afraid of what was inside
questions.explanation: The whole first paragraph establishes that only the grandmother opened that drawer. The pause is the weight of that rule ending. Choice A uses a real detail, the sticking drawer, to explain the wrong thing, which is a favourite SSAT move.

questions.stem: The photograph is significant mainly because it
choices: proves the grandmother owned a bicycle
explains why the drawer was kept shut
shows that the grandmother was forgetful
hints at a whole life the narrator knew nothing about
identifies the person outside the frame
questions.explanation: A young woman laughing at someone we never see is a glimpse of a person the narrator never met, and the last line is about never being able to ask. Choice B is tempting but the passage never links the photograph to the rule.

questions.stem: The tone of the last paragraph is best described as
questions.explanation: Wistful means quietly regretful and longing. The narrator is not angry at anyone, just aware of something now permanently out of reach. Bitter would require blame, and there is none.

questions.stem: The passage is told from the point of view of
choices: an adult looking back on childhood
a child at the time of the events
an outside observer who knows everyone's thoughts
questions.explanation: The phrase I have thought about that photograph nearly every week since, and now there is no one left to ask, can only be spoken long afterwards. Verb tense is the giveaway on point of view questions.

questions.stem: BRISK
questions.explanation: Brisk means quick and energetic, as in a brisk walk. It can also describe cold air, which is why choice C is offered, but that is a secondary sense and the SSAT wants the primary one.

questions.stem: MEAGER
questions.explanation: Meager means scanty, too little to be adequate. Generous is the antonym, and antonyms sit among the choices on this test constantly.

questions.stem: VENTURE
questions.explanation: A venture is a risky enterprise, and as a verb it means to dare to go or to dare to say. Retreat is close to the opposite.

questions.stem: PLACID
questions.explanation: Placid means calm and untroubled, used of lakes and of temperaments. Do not let the sound of the word pull you toward placard or plastic.

questions.stem: LUMINOUS
questions.explanation: Luminous means glowing or full of light. Transparent is the near miss, since both involve light, but transparent means light passes through rather than that light is given off.

questions.stem: DETER
questions.explanation: To deter is to put someone off doing something. Choice B is there purely because the two words look alike, and they are unrelated in meaning.

questions.stem: QUAINT
questions.explanation: Quaint means attractively unusual or old-fashioned. It sounds a little like quiet, which is exactly why quiet is on the list.

questions.stem: FRAGMENT
questions.explanation: A fragment is a piece broken off something larger. Choice B plays on fragrance, which shares a few letters and nothing else.

questions.stem: Petal is to flower as
questions.explanation: Build a sentence before you look at the choices: a petal is a part of a flower. A finger is a part of a hand. Choice A fails because a leaf is part of a tree, not of a forest, and the level of the whole matters.

questions.stem: Whisper is to speak as
questions.explanation: A whisper is a small, quiet version of speaking, and a sip is a small version of drinking. Choice B pairs two words that mean nearly the same thing, with no change in degree, and choice A runs the degree the wrong way.

questions.stem: Microscope is to small as
questions.explanation: A microscope is the instrument for seeing what is too small, and a telescope is the instrument for seeing what is too far. The other pairs involve the right objects but not the relationship of instrument to the problem it solves.

questions.stem: Drought is to water as
questions.explanation: A drought is a damaging shortage of water, and a famine is a damaging shortage of food. Every other choice pairs a condition with something it has plenty of, which is the reverse relationship.

questions.stem: Reluctant is to eager as
questions.explanation: Reluctant and eager are opposites, and so are cautious and reckless. The first three choices are all pairs of near synonyms, which is the standard way this test disguises an opposites analogy.

questions.stem: Chapter is to novel as
questions.explanation: A chapter is one of the named divisions a novel is built from, and a scene plays the same role in a play. Choice A has the parts the wrong way round, since letters make up words, and choice D reverses container and contained.

questions.stem: Refrigerate is to spoil as
questions.explanation: You refrigerate food to prevent it spoiling, and you vaccinate to prevent disease. Choices A and E are the opposite relationship, since watering causes growth rather than preventing it. Watch the direction, not just the topic.
Multiply as 6 x 5 = 30, then count decimal places: one in 0.6 and two in 0.05 makes three, so 0.030, which is 0.03. Counting the places is the whole technique.

questions.stem: Which of the following is greatest?
questions.explanation: As decimals: 0.583, 0.6, 0.625, 0.667 and 0.6875. The largest is 11/16. Converting to decimals is faster than finding a common denominator when the denominators have nothing in common.

questions.stem: A train travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours. At the same rate, how far will it travel in 4 hours?
questions.explanation: The rate is 150 divided by 2.5, which is 60 miles per hour, so in 4 hours it covers 240 miles. Find the unit rate first and rate problems stop being tricky.

questions.stem: If 2 to the power of n equals 32, what is n?
questions.explanation: Count the doublings: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. That is five of them, so n = 5. The choice 16 is half of 32 and choice 4 is one doubling short.

questions.stem: A bag holds 3 red, 4 blue and 5 green marbles. If one marble is drawn at random, what is the probability it is red?
questions.explanation: There are 12 marbles in total and 3 are red, so the probability is 3/12, which simplifies to 1/4. The choice 3/8 comes from using 8 as the total, which is the count of everything that is not red.

questions.stem: In a class of 42 students the ratio of girls to boys is 3 to 4. How many more boys are there than girls?
questions.explanation: The ratio makes 7 parts, so each part is 42 divided by 7, which is 6. Girls are 18 and boys are 24, a difference of 6, which is exactly one part. Read the last line carefully: the question wants the difference, not either group, and 18 and 24 are both sitting there as choices.
